opus-5.5.text:
I think it's an extraordinary moment. We're living through what may be one of the most consequential technological transitions in human history, and the field is still remarkably young. Many of the most important questions about how advanced AI will reshape the economy, international security, and the balance of power, and how we keep these systems safe and beneficial, are wide open. That means a thoughtful person entering now can have outsized influence, because the conceptual frameworks, institutions, and norms are still being built.

I'd encourage people not to think too narrowly about what "working in AI" means. There's critical technical work in alignment, interpretability, evaluations, and security. But there's equally important work in governance: policy, law, international relations, economics, and building institutions that can handle a technology moving this fast. We badly need people who can bridge those worlds, who understand the technology well enough to be credible with engineers and understand politics well enough to be effective with governments.

My advice is to build real expertise and take the problems seriously on their own terms. Pick something concrete, go deep, and stay curious about the bigger picture. Don't wait for a perfectly defined career path, because in many cases it doesn't exist yet. You may be the one who helps define it. The field rewards people who are rigorous, humble about uncertainty, and willing to update as the technology surprises us, which it will continue to do.

r001.rationale: The response calls the field young and says AI may reshape the economy, but it does not state that AI has a small current share of the economy or connect that to substantial future impact still to come.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's genuinely one of the best opportunities out there right now, and I say that carefully, because I'm aware that people in my position have a tendency to say that about whatever field they happen to be in.

But here's the case. We're at a moment where the trajectory of AI is going to shape a huge fraction of what happens this century, and the institutions, the norms, the governance structures that will determine how that goes are mostly still being built. They don't exist yet. There are maybe a few hundred people in the world working seriously on AI governance, and on the technical safety side it's larger but still small relative to the scale of the problem. So the marginal person entering the field can have outsized influence, in a way that's just not true in most mature areas.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that the field is much more open than people assume. When I started thinking about this, there wasn't really a career path. You had to sort of invent it. Now there are research organizations, there are policy roles, there are teams inside the labs, there are positions in government. The infrastructure exists, and it's growing faster than the supply of people who are prepared to fill those roles well.

Now, the honest caveat: it's a field where the problems are hard and the feedback loops are often slow. If you go into policy work, you may spend years building relationships and understanding before you see much impact. And there's a real risk of spending your time on things that feel important but turn out not to matter much. So I'd encourage people to be reflective about what they're actually contributing, rather than just being near the action.

But if you have relevant skills, whether that's technical depth, or policy experience, or just a strong analytical mind and good judgment, and you're willing to put in the work to understand the landscape, I think the expected value of entering now is very high. The window where individual contributions can shape foundational decisions isn't going to stay open forever.

r001.rationale: The response says AI will shape much of this century, but does not explain that AI currently represents a small share of the economy or that this leaves substantial economic impact still to come.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s an extraordinary opportunity, particularly for someone who wants their career to have a positive impact. AI could become one of the most consequential technologies we develop, and there are still very important questions about how to make it safe and how to govern it well.

And it’s not just an opportunity for people who want to do technical AI research. We need people who can think carefully about institutions, international cooperation, economics, and security. How do we create incentives for developers to invest in safety? How do we help governments make good decisions under uncertainty?

That said, I wouldn’t suggest that everyone should rush into AI simply because it’s important. You want to find a connection between the problems that matter and the work you can become exceptionally good at. For someone considering it now, I’d encourage some exploration: build relevant skills, work on a concrete problem, and get feedback from people whose judgment you trust. There’s a great deal of valuable work to be done.

r001.rationale: The response calls AI potentially consequential and says valuable work remains, but it does not mention AI’s current share of the economy or link that share to substantial future impact.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an extraordinary opportunity, though the right path depends a lot on the person. AI could be one of the most consequential technologies we develop, and there’s a great deal of work to do to make its development go well.

That doesn’t mean everyone should become a machine learning researcher. We also need people who can understand institutions, international politics, economics, and how organisations make decisions. A lot of the important questions sit at the intersection of those areas and the technical work.

For someone considering entering now, I’d encourage them to explore seriously: build enough technical understanding to assess the issues, try working on a concrete problem, and find people who can give them good feedback. There’s considerable uncertainty about which contributions will matter most, so developing useful skills and good judgement is especially valuable.

r001.rationale: The response calls AI potentially consequential and says there is much work to do, but does not explain that AI currently makes up a small share of the economy or that substantial economic impact remains ahead.
